Entertainment.title: James Bond: Could Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney or Jodie Comer be the next Bond girl opposite Robert Pattinson?
Entertainment.text:
After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?

What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.

He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they go for an equally big name as a ‘Bond girl’, or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.

Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".

Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."

And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?

No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya, whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.

The duo have already shared three films together this year and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.

Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".

But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.

Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".

Speculation is also growing over Pattinson’s partner, actor and singer Suki Waterhouse. She once said she’d love to play , external"a bad-ass Bond girl, external".

But there isn’t a precedent for husband-wife couples in the films, and it may be more likely that she picks up a cameo role, if indeed she wants to.

Meanwhile, TV presenter Maya Jama has picked up new interest following her storming run on Celebrity Traitors. After she quit Love Island, rumours swirled that she could be the next Bond girl - but she’s just signed a Netflix deal, so it’s unclear whether that would still be a possibility.

Another strong contender is Florence Pugh who, like Zendaya, also stars alongside Pattinson in Dune: Part Three. Earlier this week she threw her hat in the ring to be in the new Bond film - although as a villain, rather than his leading lady.

"She ticks quite a few boxes if they're looking for someone bankable," says Rose. "I could absolutely see her as a Bond woman who turns out to be the villain, someone Bond thinks is on his side, but she's actually been playing him the whole time."

Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)

Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said, external.

Other names that have been floated include Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley, Marisa Abela, Emily Blunt, Lily James, Chase Infiniti, Inde Navarrette, Simone Ashley, Deva Cassel and Ambika Mod.

And it could easily be someone totally different. Producers have previously chosen a Bond girl who isn't particularly famous yet - or is on the cusp of stardom.

The way the films have treated Bond girls "hasn't always aged well", says Rose.

Some scenes from 1960s Bond films are "basically rape", and "wouldn't fly today", said No Time To Die director Cary Fukunaga in 2021, external - referring to Thunderball and Goldfinger.

In reality, we have come a long way since then.

Over the years, producers have taken steps to usher the franchise into the modern era.

These days, the women of Bond are now much more likely to be sharp, capable equals to 007 - and what's defined as "attractive" has also evolved.

Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).

We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.

Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.

"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".

Many people say, however, there is still further to go.

Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."

"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," suggests Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”

Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.

“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and filmmaker.

"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."

More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.

“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”

None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.

"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.

But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.

“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.

Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.

But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."

There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit".

"Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

Entertainment.title: Daphne du Maurier's grandson delves into his family's history
Entertainment.text:
A set of photos of globally renowned 20th century author Daphne du Maurier has been shared by her family for the first time.

The photos show du Maurier in a series of family images, in settings including around Cornwall where she lived and did most of her writing - she died in 1989.

Her eldest grandson Paul de Zulueta found the pictures while researching a new book telling the personal story of his grandmother's artistic dynasty.

He said: "They were all tucked away in my mother's box. She said you might find this amusing - there's a box of photos here."

Du Maurier's novels which include Rebecca, Frenchman's Creek and Jamaica Inn continue to enthral readers, and often make the dark and brooding Cornish landscape central to the story.

Rebecca, written in 1938, has sold about 30 million copies worldwide and several of her novels have been made into TV shows and films.

Her grandson says writing about his ancestors and his famous grandmother has helped him understand her better.

De Zulueta was given access to du Maurier's private letters and photos, kept by his mother and his aunt.

His book Last Night I Dreamt tells of her connection to Ferryside, on the banks of the river Fowey in Cornwall, which has been a du Maurier family home for 100 years.

She first stayed there when she was 19, and it is where she wrote her first novel, The Loving Spirit.

Bodinnick, near Fowey, is also where she met her husband, Lt Gen Sir Frederick Browning, affectionately known as Tommy within the family.

When asked to pick two of the photos, De Zulueta referred to one showing the couple walking arm in arm not long after they married, and another of them in a boat.

"I like these two", he said.

"This is a particularly nice photograph of Daphne and Tommy in Fowey. Tommy my grandfather was wearing his brown leather jerkin.

"And of course this one is taken just outside of Ferryside in 1932. It must have been around the time of their honeymoon more or less, as they got married in July1932.

"So that photograph is particularly special I think."

De Zueleta visited his grandmother in Fowey as a child every school holiday.

He remembers her being great fun, very mischievous and "someone with a great sense of humour, who filled a room with laughter", rather than the reclusive figure she is often described as.

He said: "She was extraordinarily happy here.

"And she said when she first came down to Cornwall 'this is the freedom that I have long sought.

"The freedom to write and the freedom to walk, the freedom to be by myself'."

She later moved to Menabilly, the house that was the inspiration for Manderley, the country estate in Rebecca.

Rediscovering his grandparents' relationship from the perspective of an adult has been a voyage of discovery for De Zulueta, who now believes his grandfather had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder after the war, for the rest of his life.

Browning's wartime service culminated in commanding airborne forces in the flawed Operation Market Garden, where thousands of troops parachuted into the Netherlands trying to seize key bridges from the Germans.

De Zulueta now recognises the stress his grandfather's absence would have had on the couple and the pressures of war meant "we need to judge the era softly".

He said: "They [Tommy and Daphne] had a very loving, deep relationship but it was unsettled at times.

"My grandmother was bisexual and she did also have an affair in 1942."

"I think Daphne regretted that affair, the family have never admitted to it, but I discovered a letter," he added.

Her grandson said reading her correspondence meant he had "got to like her a lot more".

"I always felt Daphne neglected him and therefore I was always in my grandfather's camp, but the more I read more about her life, I began to admire and respect her a great deal more.

"She was a great writer and how could she possibly be up in London trying to write books with my grandfather."

"She had to be in Cornwall because that was the ground-swell of her imagination," he added.

Entertainment.title: How Westside Cowboy went from student gigs to rising stars in two years
Entertainment.text:
In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.

What started as jamming for fun in a student bedroom has become the latest revolution in British indie known as "Britainicana".

Now the quartet have been named the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year for 2026.

Westside Cowboy join a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan and several other now household names that have won the award.

But how did they get there, and so quickly?

It is 3 December 2024 and I am finally about to see Westside Cowboy.

A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.

It was the launch night of their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You).

It is a sub-three-minute explosion of some of the finest pop rock you could ever hope to hear.

They had released the single on 7 November 2024 and uploaded it to the BBC Introducing website on the same day.

I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.

It was soon played by Emily Pilbeam on BBC Radio 6Music.

Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.

By the time their second single Shells was released in April 2025, Westside Cowboy had been selected by BBC Introducing to play on their illustrious stage at Glastonbury festival.

The song also went straight on to the coveted 6Music playlist.

Every other single the band have released since has received the same treatment and more.

Paddy Murphy, Reuben Haycocks and Aoife Anson O'Connell met in autumn 2021 at the Royal Northern College of Music on Oxford Road.

One day, Murphy and Haycocks walked down Oxford Road to Johnny Roadhouse, a music shop fronted with an array of hanging brass instruments and full of Manchester folklore.

It has served the city's musicians since 1955.

They ran into guitar repairer, Jimmy Bradbury, who asked Murphy and Haycocks if they fancied starting a band called Westside Cowboy.

Be grateful that the answer was yes - with O'Connell joining later that evening.

Murphy and Bradbury had been in a band together before, a surf-rock trio called Katz, and Murphy and Haycocks both played in another trio, DieKaiDie.

Drummer Murphy played guitar for another band too, Holly Head, however O'Connell had not even played a guitar before she picked up the bass for Westside Cowboy. She was a cellist.

It is safe to say that this new band had plenty of competition for their time, but nevertheless it was soon to be their top priority.

It all began in Paddy's student bedroom.

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.

Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.

On 1 February 2025 I introduced them on stage.

Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.

It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.

Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.

Westside Cowboy then also won Glastonbury's prestigious Emerging Talent Competition to perform on the Woodsies Stage alongside Blossoms and Scissor Sisters.

The pinch-me moments weren't done with.

After a performance on Later… with Jools Holland on BBC Two, Westside Cowboy were off to America again to make their US television debut on The Tonight Show starring Jimmy Fallon, one of the most recognisable TV shows in the world.

It was still under two years since their first headline show.

In a world where artists fiddle frustratingly at algorithms trying to get their music to an audience on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and Spotify, this is an old school meteoric rise the likes of which the music industry must have thought no longer possible.

It has been achieved by four seemingly ordinary students regularly seen wandering down Oxford Road in Manchester.

Together the have been named the outstanding emerging act of the year by the BBC Introducing.

Entertainment.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
Entertainment.text:
A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown, which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched.

The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog. The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with collaborators.

To maid Marie, who had a sexual relationship with an occupying German officer and lives in fear of the ritualised humiliation of female “horizontal collaborators” on the streets of Copenhagen, liberation day is not the end of the terror but its start. However, the film asks, was her wartime conduct any more shameful than that of her factory-owning employer, who shored up his wealth by continuing to do business with the Germans?

May el-Toukhy’s film, out in the UK in March, is part of a raft of new high-profile productions that revisit Nazi-occupied Europe from the perspective of collaborators. Emmanuel Marre’s A Man of His Time, released in France in September as Notre Salut, tells the story of a careerist bureaucrat clambering up the administrative rungs of the Vichy regime, while Xavier Giannoli’s Les Rayons et les Ombres, or Rays and Shadows, paints a controversially sympathetic portrait of Jean Luchaire, a pacifist advocate of Franco-German reconciliation, who ended up a fervent pro-collaboration propagandist.

Resistance and collaboration are hardly taboo subjects for European film, but for most of the postwar era directors have approached them from the point of view of those who stood up against totalitarian rule: the resistance fighters of Roberto Rossellini’s Rome, Open City, filmed on the streets of the Italian capital just months after liberation; the Montmartre theatre-owners who hide Jews in their basement in François Truffaut’s The Last Metro; or a Jewish spy infiltrating Nazi ranks in Dutch director Paul Verhoeven’s Black Book. In 1974, when Louis Malle made Lacombe, Lucien, a film about a 17-year-old country boy who joins the Gestapo rather than the resistance, it scandalised France and saw the director accused of failing to choose his side.

The new generation of collaboration dramas is more comfortable in the moral grey zone. Giannoli’s film takes its inspiration from a line by Victor Hugo: “Every man on earth has two faces, Good and Evil. To blame everything is to understand nothing.” But as far-right nationalist parties are primed to win elections all over Europe next year, is there something troubling about films that revisit the 1940s and suggest we see through the eyes of those who sided with oppressors, rather than those who stood against them?

Many historians will say these films simply provide a more realistic picture of what life in Nazi-occupied Europe looked like on the ground. “One of the biggest myths people told themselves after 1945 was that Europe liberated itself,” says Halik Kochanski, whose 2023 book Resistance: The Underground War in Europe 1939-1945 was one of the first comparative studies of the subject. Armed resistance, Kochanski says, was “generally much smaller than people tend to think”, actively pursued by “no more than 5% of the population in most countries”.

The willingness, but also the ability to fight back varied from country to country. In Poland, a German policy to partition the occupied country, wipe out its intelligentsia and eradicate any signs of Polish nationhood was met by a population with a relatively recent history of uprisings and clandestine operations. Resistance was a matter of survival.

In most of western Europe, though, it was more complex. The Netherlands had no recent history of occupation, and a flat geography that made armed resistance a logistical challenge. In neutral Denmark, which the Nazis took in 1940 to attain a gateway to the Baltic Sea, the king was allowed to stay on the throne and the country was even allowed free elections. As a result, resistance remained low-key until the Germans instituted martial law in 1943.

Norway had the archetypal Nazi collaborator in puppet government leader Vidkun Quisling, and a democratic government in exile, which made its postwar reckoning straightforward. But not all of its resistance heroes have stood the test of time. Earlier this year, literary historian Narve Fulsås discovered that literature Nobel laureate Sigrid Undset, an anti-fascist icon who fled to the US when the Nazis invaded, continued to be published in Germany right up until 1940, in spite of the fact that the Nazis had Aryanised her publisher in 1936 and sent its Jewish founder to a concentration camp.

Even in France, the country that has mythologised its resistance like no other, dissent was not widespread until the Germans decreed forced labour in 1942. Like Henri Marre, the protagonist of A Man of His Time, many French people were distrustful of the occupiers but found it easy to convince themselves that working with them was in the national interest. “We can’t let the Germans call the shots,” Marre tells one of his colleagues.

Kochanski says: “The Vichy regime and the collaborating administrations in the Low Countries all said, ‘We are the shield that will protect our populations from the worst of German depredations.’ What built the resistance was that shield being broken – and people found it was their local authorities who were calling them up for forced labour and rounding up Jews.”

Even then, armed uprisings or acts of sabotage were less common than postwar cinema has made us think. This was largely because those found to be involved in resistance activity faced torture and death – and not just their own. On 10 June 1944, a German Waffen-SS unit murdered 642 civilians in the village of Oradour-sur-Glane, in retaliation for the French resistance’s nearby killing of a Nazi officer.

Kochanski recalls imposing a dilemma on a group of friends down the pub. “Imagine you lived under Nazi occupation and you decided to shelter a Jewish friend. That’s fine, you are taking that risk. Now, imagine all the people in our group agree to help you hide this friend. That’s also fine, because we’re all taking that risk. But do you have the right to cause everyone in this pub to be executed because you have decided to hide a Jew?”

Bernhard Fulda, a professor of modern history at Cambridge, sometimes asks prospective students if they would have joined the resistance in Nazi Germany. He is sceptical of those who say yes. “I have a problem with that kind of moral grandstanding,” he says. “If you haven’t lived under a dictatorship, how do you know what you would have done?”

Fulda caused a stir in Berlin in 2019 with an exhibition about the political affiliations of Emil Nolde, one of a handful of artists in the Nazis’ notorious “degenerate art” exhibition who were also fully paid-up members of the party. “How can we be certain we wouldn’t have done what most people did: trying to muddle on, keep a low profile, possibly even consider some opportunistic career moves?”

In Rays and Shadows, Jean Luchaire’s collaboration allows him to supply Jewish friends and family with paperwork enabling their escape. He even tolerates a resistance cell printing anti-Nazi leaflets in the basement. But his main motive is to maintain a lifestyle of parties and drugs.

In A Man of His Time, a story based on director Henri Marre’s real-life great-grandfather, the Vichy administrator’s promise to shield the French people turns out to be flimsy. Instead of supplying the German side with the 25 trucks they have demanded in order to vanish French Jews off to concentration camps in the east, the bureaucrat decides to give them only five trucks, with half the amount of petrol requested. “That way,” he insists, “we’ve done our best. They can’t complain.”

Resistance could be subtle and still effective. “One mistake people make,” says Kochanski, “is that they see resistance as meaning armed resistance. I see it in its broadest sense, which is really anything to harass or hamper the enemy.”

This might have been be an act as simple as a farmhand keeping a record of milk deliveries to a German military unit and passing it on to resistance cells tracking troop movements. In Norway, mass resignations among judicial and church authorities, sports associations going on strike, and ordinary citizens spamming the education ministry with protest letters all helped to spoil Quisling’s Nazification plan.

One of the most extraordinary acts of non-violent resistance took place in the Netherlands, where a group of artists calling themselves Persoonsbewijzencentrale, or Identity Card Centre, painstakingly forged the compulsory IDs the Germans had introduced to track the population. Initially intended to help out fellow artists, the plan grew until the group had forged 80,000 documents and ration cards for people in hiding. Eventually it was exposed and most of its members executed.

This cell’s activity was captured by Violette Cornelius, whose photographs are currently on display at the Nederlands Fotomuseum in Amsterdam. Since these photographs effectively identified the members of an illegal group, the negatives were buried in eastern Netherlands and only re-emerged long after the end of the war.

Cornelius was later part of a collective of photographers who documented the German occupation in the final year of the war, using cameras hidden under coats and inside shopping bags, in anticipation of an imminent reckoning after liberation day. It was the kind of heroic work missing from the current crop of collaboration dramas – but even here there was ambiguity. “Photographers played a kind of double role in the resistance,” says Loes van Harrevelt, curator of the Amsterdam show. “Some used their darkroom skills to help forge ID cards, but many also helped take the portraits for the real documents in the first place.”

For Europeans, films about the second world war are always a form of collective therapy – as much about making sense of the past as to explore, or fantasise, how we would behave in similar circumstances. Perhaps the idea of a pure act of resistance is simply inconceivable to modern minds hyper-alert to accusations of hypocrisy.

“In the 1980s,” says historian Fulda, “the moral righteousness that is required to say, ‘You guys would have supported the fascists and I wouldn’t’ came much more easily to people. But in the contemporary context, shaped by the climate crisis, finger-pointing is much harder because we know our own lifestyle choices contribute to the problem. Many people try to be eco-friendly but still fly with easyJet. Perhaps collaboration is no longer such a useful concept when everyone is complicit.”

Entertainment.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
Entertainment.text:
Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …”

The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker.

The pair are two weeks into filming series five of The Trip, the show devised by director Michael Winterbottom as a kind of blurry version of the actors’ real lives. Each season sends them on a kind of Epicurean road trip, under the guise of a journalistic commission; this time, the conceit is that Brydon is making a podcast for the Guardian, and Coogan has agreed to tag along.

Over the past 16 years, The Trip has taken them from the north of England to a meandering tour of Italy, via Spain and Greece. Now they have reached Scandinavia, heading through Sweden and Norway and up to the Arctic Circle, taking in luxury hotels, fishing huts, brown cheese and reindeer.

It has been six years since they last convened. Since then, much has happened in their lives. Brydon is an established national treasure, hosting gameshows and voicing Julia Donaldson adaptations, even writing a children’s book of his own. Coogan has combined a broad populism – revisiting his comic creation Alan Partridge and a turn in The White Lotus, with more nuanced projects – playing Jimmy Savile, for instance, and writing and producing Stephen Frears’s film The Lost King.

After breakfast, filming moves to the hotel spa, where Coogan and Brydon sit in bathrobes to record a podcast episode, their conversation drifting once again from saunas to birch twigs to an analysis of their own physiques. Meanwhile, the crew fold themselves into tight corners, hover behind camera lines, try not to laugh. All these years in, the show remains joyously funny. Still, in this quiet landscape it is hard not to notice the sense of contemplation that runs through this series; a rumination on age and friendship, pleasure, purpose, isolation and joy.

It is the following summer when we meet again: a wildly hot day in a central London hotel. By this stage, the series is finished, and Coogan has watched three episodes. “I was surprised at how much I laughed,” he says. “My memory was that it was just a bit haphazard and a bit silly, but different enough for it to be charming. What I wasn’t expecting was to find it so warm and welcoming. Throughout all the cynicism and arguments and spikiness, it has a real humanity.”

For a time they sit and discuss the moments that did not make the final cut: James Bond references, digs at other comedians, a plunge into a bracingly cold river. Some established elements of the show remain: there are the famed impressions, jabs about the directions of their respective careers, the appeal of light entertainment, the allure of politics, their differing relationships. But there are shifts in this series, too: subtle turns in subject matter, the old prickliness of their exchanges often giving way to a kind of tenderness.

They are keen, as ever, to differentiate between their onscreen relationship and a real-life friendship that has run for 30 years. These days, Brydon says the pair “get together and talk about middle-aged things”. Coogan nods. “We talk about things that are achingly middle-class preoccupations,” he says. “Things that are very, very unsympathetic.” He reels off a couple of examples: second homes, complaining about staff. “You see, when I was young and from a lower middle-class background, people used to laugh and joke and say: ‘Oh, you just can’t get the staff …’” he says. “And now I’m 60, and I’m in a different socioeconomic position, I do know what that means.”

Brydon looks up. “By the time this comes out, you’ll be 61,” he says. “It’s probably better to say 61. Let’s just say you’re mid-60s.”

Coogan frowns. “No,” he says. “Don’t say that.”

The matter of age runs through The Trip to the northern lights. Today, they talk about the subject with a kind of zeal. “What you notice is that thing of being a bit more carpe diem, a bit more living in the moment,” says Coogan. “Just trying to stand outside yourself, and celebrating if things are good.”

He noticed this growing feeling in his late 50s, though it only seemed to gather pace as he reached 60, and became a grandfather. “It’s a visceral, animal thing,” he says. “I’ve got a granddaughter, and I just want to see her, I just want to be with her, in a way that transcends all of the stuff. I want that almost like a child wants something.” He smiles. “Getting old is quite like being a child,” he says. “Children live in the moment, and they absorb, and they’re quite visceral. And I think when you get older, you start to do that too. I just want to do funny voices. And make her laugh and that’s enough.”

“What do you do for her, Neil Kinnock?” asks Brydon. “The wheels on the bus go round and round,” he sings in a recognisably Kinnockian intonation.

Coogan nods. “Yes,” he says. “Just because I know that when she gets older and she starts asking, what does it mean: ‘Hiring taxis to scuttle around handing out redundancy notices to its own workers’?”

For Brydon, 61, age has brought a sense of broadening fascination. “I’ve become interested in other things,” he says, “and I love the feeling – and this is going to look awful written down – that I’m evolving.” He speaks of a reverence for nature: birdsong, trees, the feel of his bare feet on the grass. But also for jazz and old cars. “I’m in a very fortunate position,” he says, “to have lots of opportunities to experience new things.”

“That’s the thing,” Coogan says. “Because at a certain level, where we are, we are infantilised. And that can be good and bad. The term ‘behaving like a child’ is double-edged: you can be conceited and selfish, but you can also be curious and open.”

“Which of those would you say you are?” Brydon wonders.

“Sometimes I’m spoilt and I feel like things should just be done for me,” Coogan says. “But I also feel like I’m still able to have a sense of play. Children, when they’re really young, they’re not worried if they’re cool or not, they just do things.” Sometimes, he adds, he looks at politicians young enough to be his own child, and they seem so grown up. “There’s no sense of any playfulness or childlike qualities left in them,” he says, and sighs heavily.

We meet on the day that Nigel Farage is rumoured to be triggering a byelection in his Clacton seat. “Has he resigned?” Brydon asks. “Let’s find out.” He slips into the voice of a TV news anchor. “Steve Coogan is in central London. Steve, what’s the latest on this?”

Coogan checks his phone. “Latest one hour ago. Oh, seven minutes ago. Oh, oh, oh. He’s resigned. He has resigned.” He reads Farage’s statement aloud. “Now, that’s a gamble. A bit like old Burnham’s gamble.”

“Which position will you be taking up in Andy Burnham’s cabinet?” Brydon asks him. In 2025, Coogan was appointed co-chair of the Middleton Mayoral development corporation – a move by Burnham, then still mayor of Greater Manchester, to regenerate the actor’s home town. When Burnham duly campaigned for election in the Makerfield byelection, Coogan joined him on the doorstep. “So what would it be, Defence?” Brydon continues, as Coogan explains his role in Middleton. “Secretary of state for defence, Steve Coogan?”

Coogan bats the idea away. “I am very supportive of him,” he says. “He’s trying to do something really distinctive to get away from Westminster-centric politics. I blame the rise of Reform squarely on what I would call north London intellectual liberals who are part of the cabal of centrist moderation, where they think whether you’re left or right is just an intellectual position, like a game of chess.”

He leans forward in the overstuffed armchair, gathering speed and intensity. “It’s been a game that’s been going on for the last 40 years,” he says. “And people in the provinces, in post-industrial areas, it means nothing to them and nothing has changed. The only relation to working-class people they have is when the plumber comes round. But they have no real empathy for them. And as long as we have people who seem like they’re just a sensible chap, doing a sensible job, Reform will continue to gather momentum because working-class people are fed up, they’re lashing out, they want an alternative, and there are no alternatives around. And that is squarely the fault of the Hampstead Pansies.” He pauses, breathes. “That’s it,” he says.

Brydon describes himself as “probably one of those centrists”. He is not without passion or belief, but when he speaks about his experience of life it is with more contentment than hunger. “I don’t subscribe to more, better, best,” he says. “I feel my role in life is to entertain people.” He talks of how often people approach him to thank him for his work – in Gavin & Stacey, say, or hosting Would I Lie to You? “And I’m very happy with that. I’m happy doing it. And I feel that that is what I put into the world. I try and do good. But I’m not an activist. I’m just not that person.”

It is interesting, then, to think of the young Brydon. The son of a car salesman and a teacher, he grew up in Baglan, near Port Talbot, coming of age at the height of Thatcherism, and just as the nearby steelworks was forced to lay off half its workers. There was certainly something in him that did not want to stick around; like Coogan, he applied, unsuccessfully, to Rada. Surely that shows a dream of something more or better?

“Yes,” he concedes, “in those days, of course. But success came to me later. Steve was successful in his 20s. I was 34, 35, and I had been around the block. I’d had limited success in Wales as a radio and TV personality. And by the time I met Steve, I was making a nice living – ski holidays, two cars, all that stuff – because I was a voice artist. But then it came. So I think I’ve always appreciated it more. I already had three children so I’d matured to a certain degree.”

“The thing Rob has done, what’s not often addressed, is he could have gone down the route of just being a lightweight, fringe act – someone who gets by with getting the stuff that more successful people reject,” Coogan says. “Mopping stuff up, making a living, just getting by by being affable. But, no.” There was a period, he points out, where Brydon was writing and starring in the devastatingly dark comedies Human Remains and Marion & Geoff, and simultaneously making appearances on the Home Shopping network. “The thing I’ve always said to Rob is, he’s a brilliant character actor, but he’s sort of …” he tries to find the most diplomatic way to put it, “… he’s not neglected that, but he’s …”

“Well, I did a bit,” says Brydon. “But when you talk about being content and everything, what no one ever mentions is my five children. When people talk about people’s careers, it’s as if they’re existing in a vacuum. And for me, the choices that I make are because I don’t want to go away. For the last 30 years I’ve had children growing up and the need and the want to be around. So that has been a big part of my career.”

By contrast, Coogan has one daughter, who is now 30. It has been a long time since he was bound by the restrictions of childcare and school holidays. “I do feel like I’m a bit like I’m 24 and have no responsibilities,” he says. “I’ve got a partner, but she has a career, she has another life.”

The divergent paths of their careers is sometimes puzzling to Coogan. He is confused by Brydon’s willingness to be a personality, his ease at being recognised. “You’re so accessible and approachable, they feel like they know you,” he says. Once, the pair walked together up a mountain, and as other walkers approached, Coogan found himself looking away for fear of being recognised. “But he would be face-forward, open and friendly. I would want to avoid that like the plague.” It is easier, sometimes, for him to play a role; Partridge, for example, or even the augmented version of himself we see in The Trip. “Basically, because I don’t feel entirely comfortable in my own skin,” he says.

“That’s the difference,” Brydon interjects. “I do.”

Accordingly, Brydon is quite happy with the span of his career – one week hosting ITV gameshow The Floor, the next playing Peter O’Toole in a Radio 4 drama, followed by “a big animated film” and a new sitcom, Bills Included, for Coogan co-founded production company, Baby Cow. He is never quite sure where the road will take him.

“But the joke I always say is that ‘Steve is driven. I like to be driven. In an S-Class Mercedes or equivalent.’” Coogan laughs. “It was you who said to specify that,” Brydon tells him.

“Well I don’t like people carriers,” Coogan says affably. “The Mercedes – which I wouldn’t drive, but I’d quite like to be a passenger in – is because you can make the rear seat recline. And that’s very important because I like to nap. Now that might sound like I’m a prima donna, but I do like to nap, because I’m 60.”

They joke for a moment about how they are ageing “properly”; a careful balance of somnolence and wonder. I think back to one night in Norway, when Brydon had headed off to bed, and a member of staff rushed in and urged us all to hurry outside. In the cold night air we gathered in the courtyard and looked up. There, high above the silent rooftops, the northern lights undulated across the sky: pale green and pink and golden. I remember how we stood there, quite rapt. And how I looked across at Coogan, and saw his face, lit up like a child. There in the moment, enjoying everything.

The Trip to the Northern Lights starts Thurs 10 December on Sky Atlantic & Now.

BreakingNewsTab.title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".

"That is the reality," he said on Monday.

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

Climate advocates reacted with dismay at the failure of the talks.

Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".

The COP process was "in need of significant reform", Gore wrote on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."

"It's time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world," he added.

Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.

But following the weekend's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday.

The UN climate process has "suffered setbacks before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.

He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.

Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".

"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.

He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".

He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.

She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.

May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".

Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.

Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.

She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.

Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.

Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.

On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.

He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".

He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Manchester's Co-op Live evacuated after 'unknown substance' let off in crowd
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester on Sunday night after an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd, police said.

The incident happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00.

The North West Ambulance Service said one person was taken to hospital for further assessment while more than 50 people were assessed for "eye and respiratory symptoms".

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said a major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.

Footage on social media showed emergency services converge on the arena, while some concertgoers were seen coughing as they streamed out of the venue.

In a statement early on Monday, GMP said more than 12,000 people had been safely evacuated, with several people assessed for side effects.

"Our priority was to ensure the safety of every person that was attending the concert," GMP Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said.

"Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time. Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.

"We understand the concern that this incident will have raised – particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night – and we'd like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published in full on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases," he said.

"Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary."

He added: "Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

BreakingNewsTab.title: On the streets with the French Black Block ultra left protesters
BreakingNewsTab.text:
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).

Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.

Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.

"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.

"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."

"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.

They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.

I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.

They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."

How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?

They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.

French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.

Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.

"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.

"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.

"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."

When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.

Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."

"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."

I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".

Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to bring down the French Republic?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.

"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."

You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.

"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.

"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"

How can you say that, I want to know?

"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.

But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.

"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.

Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.

Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.

The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.

France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Will it snow this week?
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK is in the grip of the coldest spell of autumn so far, but will it result in snow?

Mild Atlantic air that arrived in the south-west of the UK over the weekend is pushing eastwards, coming up against colder Arctic air.

In this setup, the meteorological ingredients for snow are in place; however, there remains uncertainty in where the boundary between the cold and mild air will sit.

Even small shifts in temperature could make a significant difference to what falls from the sky and, crucially, the chances of snow.

A clash between the air masses is already underway, as weather systems arrived from the Atlantic overnight into Sunday, bringing milder air with them.

The coming days will see the UK caught between lingering cold air, held in place by a dominant area of high pressure over Norway, and milder, wetter conditions associated with Sunday's weather fronts.

For many, the main hazards will be freezing fog and icy stretches, particularly where skies clear overnight.

Further west, rain could still bring a risk of disruption, while uncertainty remains over the potential for snow.

The key question is whether the cold air can hold its ground or whether milder Atlantic conditions will steadily push eastwards.

Monday will begin on a cold note, with temperatures widely below freezing, bringing frost along with patches of ice and freezing fog.

Blue skies and just a few fair-weather clouds will follow the frost.

Any patchy fog will clear, but with winds a little fresher than on Sunday, temperatures will reach 8 to 10C.

Meanwhile, Sunday's bands of rain will gradually weaken over southwest England and Wales, where conditions will remain grey, damp and blustery.

At times, cloud and light rain will also spread into Northern Ireland.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.

Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.

In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.

The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.

Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.

The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.

Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.

The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.

She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.

"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.

During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.

"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.

Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.

The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.

Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".

Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.
